title: Respect feature axes and training statistics
scope: Non-square array axes; provided training-only means

items.prompt: A training array X has shape (2, 3): rows are samples and columns are features. X = [[1, 4, 10], [5, 0, 13]]. Compute the per-feature means a scaler would store. Enter exact values as decimals or fractions such as 3/8; tolerance ±0.001.
items.solution: Feature means: (1 + 5)/2 = 3, (4 + 0)/2 = 2, (10 + 13)/2 = 11.5. X.mean(axis=0) has shape (3,); X.mean(axis=1) would instead give two per-sample means [5, 6].
hints: Rows are samples and columns are features, so a per-feature mean averages down each column (NumPy axis=0).
For feature 1 average the first entry of each row (1 and 5); do the same for features 2 and 3.
Feature means: (1 + 5)/2 = 3, (4 + 0)/2 = 2, (10 + 13)/2 = 11.5. X.mean(axis=0) has shape (3,); X.mean(axis=1) would instead give two per-sample means [5, 6].
items.remediation: If you averaged across a row (for example (1 + 4 + 10)/3 = 5) you reduced the feature axis; per-feature statistics reduce the sample axis. Revisit /lessons/PY04.

items.prompt: A data loader stores the TRAINING matrix feature-major with shape (3, 4): row j holds feature j for the 4 training samples. Stored = [[2, 4, 6, 0], [10, 14, 12, 16], [-1, 0, 3, 2]]. A held-out sample [13, 3, 6] arrives later. Compute the per-feature means a scaler must store, fitted on training data only. Enter exact values as decimals or fractions such as 3/8; tolerance ±0.001.
items.solution: Feature 1: (2 + 4 + 6 + 0)/4 = 3; feature 2: (10 + 14 + 12 + 16)/4 = 13; feature 3: (-1 + 0 + 3 + 2)/4 = 1. Folding the held-out sample in would give [5, 11, 2], which leaks test data into the scaler.
hints: Here each stored row is one feature, so a per-feature mean averages along each stored row (axis=1); the held-out sample is not training data.
Average the four numbers in each stored row and leave [13, 3, 6] out of every mean.

Feature 1: (2 + 4 + 6 + 0)/4 = 3; feature 2: (10 + 14 + 12 + 16)/4 = 13; feature 3: (-1 + 0 + 3 + 2)/4 = 1. Folding the held-out sample in would give [5, 11, 2], which leaks test data into the scaler.
items.remediation: [5, 11, 2] means the held-out sample was included in the fit. If you got 3.667, 6, 7, 6 (four values, one per stored sample) you averaged down the stored columns (axis=0), which mixes features. Revisit /lessons/PY04.

items.prompt: A standard scaler was fitted on training data only and stored per-feature mean = [3, 13, 1] and std = [2, 2.5, 0.5]. Standardise the held-out sample [6, 9, 0.25] with z = (x - mean)/std, feature by feature. Enter exact values as decimals or fractions such as 3/8; tolerance ±0.001.
hints: A held-out sample is transformed with the stored training mean and std; nothing is refitted on it.
For each feature subtract its stored mean, then divide by that feature's stored std (not the variance).
items.remediation: Zeros mean you refitted the mean on the held-out sample itself. -0.64 for feature 2 means you divided by the variance 6.25 instead of the std 2.5. Revisit /lessons/PY04.

items.prompt: A 2×2 RGB image uses HWC layout (height, width, channel). Its four pixels in row-major order are [[10, 200, 30], [20, 180, 50], [30, 160, 40], [60, 140, 80]]. Compute the three channel means by reducing height and width while keeping the channel axis. Enter exact values as decimals or fractions such as 3/8; tolerance ±0.001.
hints: Channel means reduce the spatial axes H and W and keep C; each output averages one channel over all pixels.
Collect the four red values (first entry of each pixel) and average them; repeat for green and blue.
items.remediation: If you got one number per pixel (for example 80 for the first pixel) you averaged the three channels together. Revisit /lessons/PY04.

items.prompt: A training batch has shape (2, 1, 2, 3) in NHWC layout: two images, each 1×2 pixels with RGB channels. Image 1 pixels: [0, 50, 255], [40, 70, 205]. Image 2 pixels: [80, 90, 155], [120, 10, 105]. Compute the dataset channel means used for normalisation (one value per channel). Enter exact values as decimals or fractions such as 3/8; tolerance ±0.001.
hints: Dataset channel statistics reduce every axis except C: batch N, height H and width W.
List the four red values across both images and average them; repeat for green and blue.
items.remediation: If you produced one set of means per image (for example red 20 and 100) you kept the batch axis N; dataset channel statistics reduce it too. Revisit /lessons/PY04.

items.prompt: Training images gave stored channel statistics mean = [120, 110, 100] and std = [60, 50, 40] (R, G, B). Normalise the held-out test pixel [150, 85, 160] channel by channel with z = (x - mean)/std. Enter exact values as decimals or fractions such as 3/8; tolerance ±0.001.
hints: Each channel uses its own stored training mean and std; the test pixel does not change the statistics.
For each channel subtract that channel's stored mean, then divide by that channel's stored std.
items.remediation: If all three values used the same mean or std you mixed channels; each channel keeps its own statistics. Recomputing a mean from the test pixel itself is a train/test leak. Revisit /lessons/PY04.

routeNotes.feature-columns: Reduce the sample axis of non-square feature matrices, fit on training rows only, and apply stored statistics to a held-out row.
routeNotes.image-channels: Reduce spatial and batch axes while preserving RGB, then normalise a held-out pixel with stored training channel statistics.
